title: Popocatépetl erupting in 2017
author: SchneidIt (David Schneider)
alt: Popocatepetl erupting in 2017, photographed from UNAM in Mexico City
caption: A modern eruption photographed in 2017. This is not an image of the ancient Lorenzo eruption.
support: A real ash plume makes explosive volcanism a process worth testing in the destruction account. The connection is a geological hypothesis; the text does not name this volcano.
limit: The latest Lorenzo estimate is approximately 40 calibrated BCE; full probability tables remain unaudited here. No Book of Mormon identification follows from this modern photograph.

title: Ilopango caldera lake
author: JMRAFFi
alt: Lake Ilopango caldera seen from the panoramic road
caption: The modern lake occupies Ilopango caldera. Its famous Tierra Blanca Joven eruption is dated centuries after AD 33-34.
support: This caldera shows the scale of a real volcanic landscape. Its dated eruption helps test—and reject—that specific eruption as the first-century destruction event.
limit: The Tierra Blanca Joven eruption is dated to AD 431 plus or minus 2 years. It does not match the first-century target.
researchTitle: Tierra Blanca Joven dated to AD 431 (2020)
eventDate: Tierra Blanca Joven: AD 431 ± 2 · later event

author: José Macías
license: Provider states Usage Restrictions: No; License: Original content. This is an explicit provider permission statement, not a Creative Commons license.
alt: Actual excavation of Tetimpa settlement beneath volcanic deposits, as identified by Geological Society of America.
caption: Tetimpa excavation, photographed in 1995. A real settlement buried by Popocatépetl deposits; its identification with a Book of Mormon city remains unestablished.
support: Excavated houses beneath volcanic deposits show that settlement burial is a real regional process. This is a stronger physical comparison than a volcano photograph alone, though the city identity and target date remain unestablished.

title: A village preserved beneath volcanic ash
author: Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz (Mariordo)
alt: Structure 3, Area 3, Joya de Cerén archaeological site, El Salvador.
caption: Structure 3 at Joya de Cerén, photographed in 2012. A later volcanic-burial analogue, not an AD 33–34 destruction site.
support: Walls and the surrounding ash layers preserve a buried village in physical detail. They help explain how a settlement can survive below ground for archaeologists to recover.
limit: UNESCO places the burial around AD 600/seventh century, centuries after the destruction account. This is a later analogue, not a candidate identification. The village was buried by Loma Caldera, a different event from Ilopango’s Tierra Blanca Joven eruption.
researchTitle: UNESCO: Joya de Ceren archaeological site
eventDate: Burial around AD 600 / seventh century; later analogue

title: Lake Atitlán · testing the inundation proposal
author: chensiyuan
alt: Lake Atitlán and volcanic slopes with San Antonio Palopó in the foreground
caption: The modern lake landscape, with San Antonio Palopó in the foreground. This photograph does not show the underwater ruins of Samabaj.
support: Underwater excavation at Samabaj makes inundation a concrete archaeological question in this lake. The landscape helps explain why investigators examine changes in water level.
limit: The excavators' approximate AD 300 chronology is pottery-based, not a directly measured flooding year. No first-century Jerusalem identification is established. This inland lake is also different from Moroni's coastal sinking account.
evidenceType: Lake landscape; underwater ruins are not visible
changes: Previously resized for the atlas; no archaeological features added.
